title: Little Caughnawaga — Mohawk Brooklyn
summary: From the 1920s to the 1960s, Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake and their families made Boerum Hill their home. Known as Little Caughnawaga, it was the largest Mohawk community outside Canada, and its men helped raise New York’s bridges and skyscrapers.
address_label: Pacific Street at Nevins Street, Boerum Hill, Brooklyn, NY
map_geometry_source: OpenStreetMap contributors, shared node of Pacific Street and Nevins Street (40.685451, -73.983092), inside the Court Street–Fourth Avenue–State Street–Douglas Street area described by Brooklyn Public Library; retrieved October 31, 2026.
why_this_matters: Native Brooklyn did not end in the 1600s. In the twentieth century, Mohawk families built a community here while their work raised the city’s skyline.
introduction_content:
For more than three decades from the 1920s, Mohawk families from Kahnawake, near Montreal, made this part of Boerum Hill their home away from home. The area bounded by Court Street, Douglas Street, Fourth Avenue and State Street became known as Little Caughnawaga, the largest Mohawk community outside Canada.[1]

Robert Grumet, writing in 1986, called it the “closely knit Mohawk community in North Gowanus.” Its men helped build many of the bridges and skyscrapers on the New York skyline.[2]
history_content:
From the Victoria Bridge to New York

Mohawk ironwork goes back to the mid-1800s, when the Victoria Bridge was built across the St. Lawrence River with its north abutment on Mohawk land. To build there, the railway hired Mohawk men and trained them in riveting. The skills passed from fathers to sons, nephews and cousins.[1]

A treaty right to cross the border

In 1926 Paul Diabo, a Mohawk ironworker, was arrested in Philadelphia as an illegal alien. His defense rested on the Treaty of Ghent, and his victory meant Mohawk workers could travel and work in both countries. Ironworkers could now bring their families, and the Brooklyn community grew.[1]

Neighborhood life

Families lived here from October to June. The Wigwam bar on Nevins Street and the Spar on Atlantic Avenue served as community centers, where men traded news of jobs and of home. Children attended P.S. 47 and Nathan Hale Junior High.[1]

At Cuyler Presbyterian Church, 360 Pacific Street, the Reverend David Cory learned his parishioners’ Iroquoian language and preached in it one Sunday evening each month. With Mohawk parishioners he translated a hymnal, and he taught after-school language classes.[1]

Moving on

By the late 1950s an estimated 500 to 700 Mohawk people lived in Brooklyn. As the building boom ended, men looked for work elsewhere in the United States and Canada, and by the 1970s little remained of Little Caughnawaga.[1] Grumet dates the fall in local demand for Mohawk skills to the 1960s.[2]

Long before, this was Lenape land along Gowanus. See also Prospect Park.
whereintheworld_content: The green dot marks Pacific Street at Nevins Street, inside the old Little Caughnawaga area.[3] The former Cuyler Presbyterian Church on Pacific Street is now a private residence; view it from the sidewalk only.[1] The Mohawk-built skyline, from the Empire State Building to the George Washington Bridge, belongs to this story too.[1]
